items.q: A business raises its price by 8%. Quantity demanded falls by 12%. What is the price elasticity of demand?
items.why: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = -12 ÷ 8 = -1.5.
items.label: Calculate

items.q: A café raises the price of a lunch deal from £5.00 to £5.50. Daily sales fall from 400 to 376. What is the PED?
items.label: Calculate

items.q: What happens to the café's daily revenue from the lunch deal?
opts: It falls, because fewer lunch deals are sold
It rises from £2,000 to £2,068, because demand is price inelastic
It stays the same, because the price rise and the fall in sales cancel out
It rises by 10%, the same as the price
items.why: Before: 400 × £5.00 = £2,000. After: 376 × £5.50 = £2,068. With inelastic demand, the higher price more than makes up for the fall in sales.
items.label: Use the answer

items.q: The PED for a product is -2.5. The business cuts its price by 4%. What is the change in quantity demanded?
opts: A rise of 10%
A rise of 6.5%
A fall of 10%
A rise of 1.6%
items.why: % change in quantity = PED × % change in price = -2.5 × -4 = +10%.
items.label: Calculate

items.q: A business sells 30,000 units. PED is -0.8. It raises its price by 5%. How many units will it now sell?
items.label: Calculate

items.q: A shop sells 1,000 units a week at £10. PED is -2. It cuts the price to £9. What is the new weekly revenue?
items.why: The price falls by 10%, so quantity rises by -2 × -10 = 20%, to 1,200 units. Revenue = 1,200 × £9 = £10,800.
items.label: Calculate

items.q: Revenue rises by £800 a week after the price cut. Why might profit not rise by the same amount?
opts: Revenue and profit are always the same
Profit always falls when price is cut
PED only affects profit, not revenue
The shop has to buy or make 200 extra units each week, which adds to its costs
items.why: Profit = revenue − costs. Selling 200 more units means more stock or materials, so costs rise too. Whether profit goes up depends on the cost of each extra unit.
items.label: Use the answer

items.q: Average incomes rise by 4%. Demand for a product rises by 6%. What is its income elasticity of demand?
items.why: YED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income = 6 ÷ 4 = +1.5.
items.label: Calculate

items.q: Incomes rise by 5% and demand for a budget brand falls by 2%. What is the YED?
items.label: Calculate

items.q: What does a YED of -0.4 tell the business selling the budget brand?
opts: Demand does not change at all when income changes
It is a luxury, so demand is very sensitive to income
The business should raise its price
It is an inferior good, so demand is likely to rise when incomes fall
items.why: A negative YED means an inferior good. If incomes fall, for example in a recession, customers switch towards it and demand rises.
items.label: Use the answer

items.q: A product has a YED of +2.2. Incomes are expected to fall by 3%. The business sells 50,000 units. What is the expected sales volume?
items.label: Calculate

items.q: Which response makes most sense for the business selling the product with a YED of +2.2?
opts: Plan for lower sales, for example by reducing production or targeting customers whose incomes are less likely to fall
Raise the price, because income elastic products always have inelastic demand
Expect sales to rise, because the YED is positive
Do nothing, because YED only matters when incomes rise
items.why: A large positive YED means demand falls sharply when incomes fall. The business should plan for this rather than assume sales will hold up.
items.label: Use the answer

items.q: The price of a product rises from £3.60 to £3.96. What is the percentage increase?
items.label: Calculate

items.q: A business spends £60,000 on a marketing campaign. It estimates the campaign made £84,000 of profit. What is the return on marketing spend?
items.why: Return on marketing spend = profit from marketing activities ÷ amount of marketing spend × 100 = 84,000 ÷ 60,000 × 100 = 140%.
items.label: Calculate

items.q: A second campaign cost £40,000 and made £50,000 of profit. Which statement is right?
opts: You cannot compare them because they cost different amounts
The first campaign gave a better return (140% compared with 125%), although the profit figures are only estimates
The second campaign was better because it cost less
The second campaign gave a higher return
items.why: 50,000 ÷ 40,000 × 100 = 125%, lower than 140%. Return on marketing spend lets you compare campaigns of different sizes, but the profit is usually an estimate, so treat the comparison with care.
items.label: Use the answer
